members.statement: Equip technical translators with technical communication, usability, subject, research, genre, and writing competence.
Train technical translators in technical communication and treat technical translation as information design and engineering.

Be a good technical writer in order to be a good technical translator — their principal stylistic goals coincide — and adopt technical writers' writing strategies and audience-analysis methods, while accepting that information design, typography, and layout are usually beyond the translator's remit.
Build or infer a robust translation brief covering intended use, audience, publication status, terminology, style constraints, legal constraints, and document conventions.

Base translation decisions on who will read the text, how they will use it, and how it will be distributed, and establish these via a translation brief specifying at minimum the target audience, the intended purpose (information vs publication), and any stylistic or terminological requirements.
Distinguish technical translation from adjacent specialized domains before choosing strategy or evaluating success.
Choose technical-translation strategy from the communicative situation and project criteria rather than universal maxims.
Use reader evidence, usability studies, and style guidance to judge what the target audience will accept as good technical documentation.
Subject user documentation to legal, standards, accuracy, completeness, safety, readability, layout, and hands-on usability quality assurance.
Treat technical documentation as collaborative designed communication whose tools, formats, roles, and purposes affect translation work.

Treat scientific and technical translation as a communicative service for people and produce a target text that functions as an authentic target-language document, because users care most about accessing its information effectively.
Evaluate user guides holistically with representative task-based usability testing; readability formulas are only partial indicators.
Treat the user guide as part of overall system usability and judge guide quality holistically.
Measure satisfaction and retention with instruments that fit the study cost, realism, and time constraints.
Measure retention, task time, error rates, and satisfaction with explicit instruments and report the aggregate outcomes.

Treat scientific and technical terminology as potentially metaphorical and culture-bound, and recognize and negotiate such metaphors much as a literary translator would, because style, metaphor, and creativity are intrinsic to scientific discourse.

Expect scientific texts to use a broader range of linguistic devices (longer, more complex sentences, figurative language) because they aim to create an effect, and treat metaphors as a valuable tool in both scientific and technical texts for naming abstractions and explaining processes through readers' existing knowledge.
When a client provides no meaningful brief, construct a working one by asking a few probing questions (such as whether the text is for publication) before translating.

Accept that the translation brief has no settled form and often forces educated guesses, so ask the client a short standard set of questions — kept small so as not to seem unprofessional, since the translator is usually the expert — covering at minimum the target language variety, the purpose (information vs publication), the deadline, and any required terminology.
Check the customer's website to capture the look and feel of their own documents, even when they state no specific language requirements, so the translation reads like one of the client's documents.
When a client needs to decide whether to commission a full translation, provide a gist (indicative) translation that conveys the basic meaning without stylistic polish.

Determine first what type of translation the client wants, because it drives what is translated, how, and how long it takes: a selective translation renders only certain sections; a gist translation is a rough summary needing less care over style; an information-purposes translation must convey all the information but tolerates rough style for internal use; and a publication-purposes translation demands the best content and flawless language, often with a second reviewer.

In guides — advanced material for readers who already have a basic understanding — adapt the plentiful examples to the target-language culture while retaining the detailed descriptions, figures, tables, and diagrams.

Treat user guides as structured instructional documents in simple language supported by graphics whose usability rests on broadly universal human cognition but also carries culture-specific features and rarely targets a single culture, so translating them is not always straightforward.

Treat a case study as a marketing text with a standard structure (identify the client, its needs as the 'problem', the solution and its implementation, a testimonial, and closing company details) that is demanding to translate because it mixes complex technical data with opinion, reported speech, and persuasion, and its language must stay positive without overstating or misrepresenting the product.

Treat a technical case study as a promotional text combining technical, marketing, and journalistic language, with a standard headline/testimonial/problem/solution structure, whose language must reflect a positive client experience without overstating or misrepresenting the product.

Understand that literal translation is more sophisticated than word-for-word replacement — shifting from word to group to clause once the target stops complying with target-language grammar, and avoiding additions, omissions, and paraphrasing — and is in fact one of the most frequently used strategies in technical texts.
Favour paraphrasing as perhaps the most useful procedure for technical translation, because it avoids interference and unidiomatic constructions caused by sticking too closely to the source text.

Establish whether the job is an instrumental translation (used in place of the source as a freestanding target text — so errors must be corrected) or a documentary translation (describing what the source said and how, as in back-translation or judicial use — so errors are preserved and shown, and back-translation is a limited quality check); in an instrumental translation the translator, as the expert, corrects simple linguistic errors, incorrect line breaks, text-versus-diagram mismatches, and obviously wrong units of measure (e.g. a 250 kg tablet where kg should be mg).

Expect source texts to contain errors (living texts are faulty texts), and decide whether to correct or preserve them by finding out from the client whether the job is instrumental or documentary; treat subject and factual errors as the trickiest category, since detecting them depends on your own subject knowledge and some standards (such as Germany's DIN 2345) place responsibility for source errors on the client.
Treat a publication-purpose translation as generally instrumental (so errors should be fixed), but do not assume an information-purpose text is documentary.
